intro: Routes, flights and ships, kinds of accommodation and the mishaps of a long trip.
p.el parador: the state-run hotel in a historic building
b1.texto:
**The route.** **La ruta**, **el itinerario**, **el trayecto** (one leg of the journey). **Recorrer** un país (to travel all over it), **atravesar** or **cruzar** el océano, **dar la vuelta al mundo**.

**Kinds of trip.** **Un viaje de negocios**, **de placer**, **de novios**. **Turismo rural**, **cultural**, **de aventura**. **Un crucero**.

**By air.** **Un vuelo directo** or **con escala**; **nacional** or **internacional**. **Hacer escala en** Lisboa. **Embarcar** and **desembarcar**. **La tripulación** looks after **los pasajeros**. A flight can be **anunciado**, **retrasado** or **cancelado**.

**At the border.** **Cruzar la frontera**, **pasar la aduana**, **declarar** what you are carrying, **pasar el control**.

**Luggage.** **Facturar**, **registrar** (to search), **extraviar**: **me han extraviado la maleta**. You can leave bags in **la consigna**.

**Where to sleep.** **Un hotel**, **un hostal**, **un albergue** (cheap, shared), **un parador** (a state-run hotel in a castle, convent or palace: a Spanish institution), **una casa rural**, **un bungaló**. Or you **acampas** and **montas la tienda de campaña**.

**The verbs.** **Alojarse en**, **registrarse**, **tener vistas a**, **dar a**.

**By sea.** **Un barco de vela**, **un ferry**, **un barco pesquero**. **Marearse** is what happens to bad sailors.
b2.f0: At fifty, Ignacio left his job to go round the world without getting on a plane.
b2.f1: He had worked out an itinerary of eight months, but the journey ended up lasting almost twice that.
b2.f2: He crossed Europe and Asia by train, staying in hostels and, when there were none, camping wherever he could.
b2.f3: The hardest leg was the Pacific one: it took him a month to find a cargo ship that would take passengers.
b2.f4: The crew, of six nationalities, adopted him at once, although he spent the first week seasick.
b2.f5: At one customs post they searched his backpack for hours, and at another they mislaid his passport.
b2.f6: When he is asked whether he would do it again, he answers that, had he known what awaited him, he would not have set off, and that this is why he is glad not to have known.
b4.pregunta: According to the text, what was the hardest part of the journey?
b4.o0.refuerzo: El trayecto más difícil fue el del Pacífico.
b4.o1.refuerzo: He did that without great trouble.
b4.o2.refuerzo: That was a problem, but not the hardest part.
b5.pregunta: According to the text, how long did the trip take?
b5.o0.refuerzo: Eight months planned, and almost double in the end.
b5.o2.refuerzo: That was the wait for a ship.
b7.pregunta: Complete: the flight stops over in Madrid.
b8.pregunta: Complete: a ship that would take passengers.
b8.o0.refuerzo: An unknown thing in the past: imperfect subjunctive.
b8.o1.refuerzo: He did not know such a ship: subjunctive.
b8.o2.refuerzo: The main verb is past, so the imperfect subjunctive.
b9.o1: They have taken out my suitcase.
b10.traduccion: We travelled the country from north to south.
b11.texto:
**The app cannot check this part.** For the writing, please use pen and paper. For the speaking, say it out loud and, if you can, practise with a native speaker or a teacher who can correct you.

**Write (150–180 words).** Write a travel article about a long journey, real or imagined, with its route, incidents and people.

**Speak (about 3 minutes).** Tell aloud the worst travel experience of your life, with all the details.
